---
title: "Time aggregation"
---

The paper's second result is what goes wrong when an econometrician
ignores time aggregation. Forcing $h = 1$ says the agent decides once
a year, the sampling interval of the data. The persistent growth shock
then looks like short-run noise, risk aversion is inflated, and the
model is rejected. This page holds Tables 4 to 6 and Figure 2. The
market fit itself is on [Estimation](estimation.qmd).

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
from great_tables import GT

from geap.lrr.estimation import (
    TABLE_5_ANNUAL_MODEL,
    TABLE_5_ANNUAL_RESIDUALS,
    estimate_bky,
    figure2_ggplot,
    figure2_irf,
    load_annual,
    long_run_variance_share,
    table3_compare,
    table4_annual_on_lrr_sims,
    table4_frame,
    table6_frame,
)

KIKU_GT = dict(table_background_color="transparent", table_font_size="0.92rem",
               heading_title_font_size="1.05rem", heading_subtitle_font_size="0.85rem",
               source_notes_font_size="0.8rem", column_labels_font_weight="bold",
               data_row_padding="4px")


def fmt_params(gt, tab):
    """Two decimals for the large parameters, four for the rest, scientific for sigma_w."""
    idx = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(tab["parameter"])}
    two = [idx[n] for n in ("gamma", "psi", "phi_d", "phi_d_sigma", "h", "J") if n in idx]
    three = [idx[n] for n in ("rho_d", "p") if n in idx]
    sci = [idx[n] for n in ("sigma_w",) if n in idx]
    four = [i for i in range(len(tab)) if i not in two + three + sci]
    num = [c for c in tab.columns if c != "parameter"]
    return (
        gt.fmt_number(columns=num, rows=four, decimals=4)
        .fmt_number(columns=num, rows=two, decimals=2)
        .fmt_number(columns=num, rows=three, decimals=3)
        .fmt_scientific(columns=num, rows=sci, decimals=2)
        .sub_missing(missing_text="")
    )


def fmt_moments(gt, tab):
    idx = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(tab["moment"])}
    sci = [idx[n] for n in ("e_eta_x", "e_eta2_s2") if n in idx]
    rest = [i for i in range(len(tab)) if i not in sci]
    num = [c for c in tab.columns if c != "moment"]
    levels = [c for c in num if not c.startswith("t_diff")]
    tstats = [c for c in num if c.startswith("t_diff")]
    gt = gt.fmt_number(columns=num, rows=rest, decimals=3)
    gt = gt.fmt_scientific(columns=levels, rows=sci, decimals=1)
    if tstats:
        gt = gt.fmt_number(columns=tstats, rows=sci, decimals=3)
    return gt.sub_missing(missing_text="")


panel = load_annual()
```

## Table 4: the annual specification

The CUE surface at $h = 1$ has several local minima. The fit below is
the lowest objective of six generic starts that differ in the IES and
in how consumption risk splits between the persistent and the short-run
shock. The simulated columns re-estimate the annual specification on
samples drawn from an LRR economy. The paper draws from its Table 2
estimates; we draw from the monthly fixed-frequency fit of Table 6 on
this page, twenty samples of 86 years, and fit each with the same CUE
as the empirical column from a single start.

```{python}
ann = estimate_bky(panel, h=1, n_starts=6)
fits = {h: estimate_bky(panel, h=h, n_starts=3) for h in (26, 12, 4)}
fits[1] = ann
mc = table4_annual_on_lrr_sims(
    n_draws=20, years=86, seed=0, lrr_params=fits[12].params, lrr_h=12
)
tab4 = table4_frame(ann, mc)
empirical = tab4[["parameter", "hat", "se_hat", "paper", "se_paper"]]
fmt_params(
    GT(empirical)
    .tab_header(title="Table 4, empirical data. Annual specification, h = 1")
    .cols_label(parameter="", hat="estimate", se_hat="SE", paper="paper", se_paper="paper SE")
    .tab_source_note("Paper: BKY (2016) Table 4, first two columns."),
    empirical,
).tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
```

```{python}
simulated = tab4[["parameter", "ours_p5", "ours_p50", "ours_p95",
                  "paper_pop", "paper_p5", "paper_p50", "paper_p95"]]
simulated = simulated[simulated["parameter"] != "h"]
fmt_params(
    GT(simulated)
    .tab_header(title="Table 4, simulated data. Annual specification on LRR samples")
    .tab_spanner(label="Ours, 20 draws", columns=["ours_p5", "ours_p50", "ours_p95"])
    .tab_spanner(label="Paper", columns=["paper_pop", "paper_p5", "paper_p50", "paper_p95"])
    .cols_label(parameter="", ours_p5="5%", ours_p50="50%", ours_p95="95%",
                paper_pop="population", paper_p5="5%", paper_p50="50%", paper_p95="95%")
    .tab_source_note("Ours: CUE on 20 draws of 86 years from the h = 12 economy below. Paper: BKY (2016) Table 4, simulated columns."),
    simulated,
).tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
```

## Table 5: moments of the annual specification

```{python}
tab5 = table3_compare(panel, ann, {**TABLE_5_ANNUAL_MODEL, **TABLE_5_ANNUAL_RESIDUALS})
fmt_moments(
    GT(tab5)
    .tab_header(title="Table 5. Moments of the annual specification")
    .cols_label(moment="", sample="sample", model="model", t_diff="t(diff)", paper_model="paper model")
    .tab_source_note("Sample and model at the Table 4 estimates. Paper: BKY (2016) Table 5 model column."),
    tab5,
).tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
```

## Figure 2: impulse responses

An ARMA(8, 8) is fitted to a long simulated annual sample of consumption
growth and of its squared deviation, under the monthly fixed-frequency
fit and under the annual specification. Panel (a) is the cumulative
response of consumption growth, panel (b) the response of the
conditional variance.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 2. Impulse responses of annual consumption growth (a) and of its conditional variance (b) under the LRR model at h = 12 (solid) and the annual specification (dashed), from ARMA(8, 8) fits to 800 simulated years."
irf = figure2_irf(years=800, seed=0, lrr_params=fits[12].params, lrr_h=12, annual_params=ann.params)
figure2_ggplot(irf)
```

```{python}
print(irf.loc[[20, 40], ["dc_lrr", "dc_annual"]].to_string())
```

## Table 6: fixed decision frequencies

Bi-weekly is $h = 26$, monthly 12, quarterly 4, annual 1. The annual
column is the Table 4 fit.

```{python}
tab6 = table6_frame(fits)
fmt_params(
    GT(tab6)
    .tab_header(title="Table 6. Model estimates with fixed decision frequency")
    .tab_spanner(label="Bi-weekly", columns=["hat_26", "paper_26"])
    .tab_spanner(label="Monthly", columns=["hat_12", "paper_12"])
    .tab_spanner(label="Quarterly", columns=["hat_4", "paper_4"])
    .tab_spanner(label="Annual", columns=["hat_1", "paper_1"])
    .cols_label(parameter="", hat_26="ours", paper_26="paper", hat_12="ours", paper_12="paper",
                hat_4="ours", paper_4="paper", hat_1="ours", paper_1="paper")
    .tab_source_note("Paper: BKY (2016) Table 6."),
    tab6,
).tab_options(**KIKU_GT)
```

```{python}
for h in (26, 12, 4, 1):
    print(f"h = {h:2d}  long-run share of var(dc) {long_run_variance_share(fits[h].params, h):.2f}")
```

::: {.firewall}
Every "paper" column is quoted from Bansal, Kiku, and Yaron (2016),
Tables 4 to 6 and Figure 2. Everything else is computed by the cell
above it. Our $J$ statistics reject the annual and quarterly
specifications as the paper's do, but they are an order of magnitude
smaller than the printed ones; the difference in the weighting and the
covariance estimator is not resolved. The annual fit is the lowest of
six generic starts; a start at the paper's printed Table 4 vector
reaches a lower objective still, with persistence 0.87 and a larger
short-run loading, so the surface has basins our starts do not reach.
The simulated columns of Table 4 rest on 20 draws, each fitted from
one start. `NUMBERS.md` lists the open caveats.
:::
